messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq Mansouri is a seventy-five-year-old widowed sculptor of Iranian descent who was referred for psychological assessment following a life-threatening accident that occurred fourteen months ago. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 75, indicating severe posttraumatic stress, and has been reluctant to engage with mental health services until now, having spent the intervening period attempting to manage his distress through his own means.

The accident occurred on an unremarkable Tuesday afternoon when Tariq was working alone in his studio, a converted warehouse on the outskirts of the city where he has produced large-scale stone and metal works for nearly four decades. A hydraulic lifting arm used to position heavy stone slabs failed without warning, and a piece of marble weighing several hundred pounds fell, striking him across the lower back and pinning him partially beneath it. He lay on the cold concrete floor for nearly two hours before a delivery driver found him. During that time, he was conscious, unable to move, and convinced — with a certainty he describes as absolute — that he was dying. He remembers the particular quality of the light through the high studio windows, the smell of stone dust, and the sensation of his own heartbeat as something frightening rather than reassuring, as though each beat might simply stop.

He survived with significant spinal injuries requiring surgery and a prolonged rehabilitation. Physically, his recovery has been partial. He walks with a cane, experiences chronic pain, and has been told by his orthopedic surgeon that certain limitations are permanent. It is this word — permanent — that has lodged itself at the center of Tariq's psychological world. He has come to believe, with a thoroughness that shapes nearly every hour of his day, that his body has been fundamentally and irreversibly damaged. He does not experience this as an adjustment to new circumstances but as a verdict: that the man who entered that studio on that Tuesday no longer exists, replaced by a diminished and untrustworthy version. He is certain he can no longer rely on his body to do what he asks of it, and the memory of the hydraulic arm — of a mechanism he trusted completely and that failed completely — has become a template through which he now reads every physical sensation.

It is precisely these appraisals of permanent damage and bodily unreliability that have driven Tariq toward a set of strategies that now govern his daily life. Because he believes his body cannot be trusted, he monitors it constantly — cataloguing twinges, tracking his breathing after mild exertion, pausing mid-movement to assess whether a sensation in his lower back represents the ordinary ache of his injury or the onset of something catastrophic. He spends considerable time each day in this internal surveillance, and the studio, once a place of physical absorption and creative freedom, has become a site of careful self-management. He no longer lifts anything heavier than a few kilograms, has stopped working with stone entirely, and declines commissions that would require him to stand for extended periods. What had been a practice built on the physical encounter between his body and resistant materials has contracted to small clay studies he works on seated. Several long-standing professional relationships have quietly dissolved as he has turned down collaborative projects, and a gallery that had represented him for twenty years has not been in contact since he declined their last exhibition invitation.

Alongside this physical withdrawal, Tariq returns repeatedly to the question of why this happened to him. He thinks about it in the evenings, in the specific silence of a house he has lived in alone since his wife died six years ago. He is not a religious man in any formal sense, but he searches for a meaning that would make the accident intelligible — some failure of attention, some accumulated carelessness — because the alternative, that it was simply random, feels to him more frightening than culpability would.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a conversation with his eldest daughter, who visited in the spring and told him, carefully, that she no longer recognized how he spent his days. He is not sure what he hopes for. What he fears most is being told that this is simply what seventy-five feels like after an injury — that there is no distinction left between damage and age, between the accident and the man.
